blocks.text: A sorted array supports binary search in $O(\log n)$ but insertion in $O(n)$. A linked list supports insertion in $O(1)$ but search in $O(n)$. The binary search tree is the structure that asks whether you can have both — and the answer, it turns out, depends entirely on one number: the height.

blocks.markdown:
## Rooted tree terminology

A **rooted tree** is a set of nodes with one distinguished **root**, in which every other node has exactly one parent and there are no cycles. A **binary** tree restricts each node to at most two children, distinguished as *left* and *right* — and the distinction matters even when only one child is present.

- **Depth** of a node: the number of edges from the root to it. The root has depth 0.
- **Height** of a node: the number of edges on the longest path from it down to a leaf. A leaf has height 0.
- **Height of the tree**: the height of the root.
- **Leaf** (external node): a node with no children. **Internal node**: a node with at least one child.
- **Subtree** rooted at $v$: $v$ together with all its descendants.
- **Size**: the number of nodes.

Be explicit about the height convention. Counting *edges* is standard in the algorithms literature and is used throughout this lesson; some texts count *nodes* on the path, giving values one larger.

blocks.title: Height bounds the size, and therefore the cost
blocks.text: A binary tree of height $h$ has at least $h + 1$ nodes (a chain) and at most $2^{h+1} - 1$ nodes (a perfect tree). Inverting the upper bound, a tree of $n$ nodes has height at least $\lceil \log_2(n+1) \rceil - 1$. Every BST operation costs $O(h)$, so the whole engineering problem is keeping $h$ near that logarithmic floor.

blocks.caption: The attainable range of heights for a binary tree on n nodes: balanced at the left end, a degenerate chain at the right

blocks.markdown:
## The ordering invariant

A **binary search tree** is a binary tree in which, for every node $v$:

> every key in the **entire** left subtree of $v$ is less than $v$'s key, and every key in the **entire** right subtree of $v$ is greater.

The word *entire* carries the weight. A weaker, local condition — merely that the left child is smaller and the right child larger — is not sufficient, and the difference is not academic. Consider root 50 with left child 30 whose *right* child is 60. Every parent–child pair is locally ordered, yet a search for 60 compares with 50, goes right, and never finds it. The global invariant is what licenses discarding a whole subtree after a single comparison.

Our running example, built by inserting 50, 30, 70, 20, 40, 60, 80:

```
            50
          /    \
        30      70
       /  \    /  \
     20   40  60   80
```

Size 7, height 2, four leaves. This is a *perfect* tree: every level is full, so $n = 2^{h+1} - 1 = 2^3 - 1 = 7$.

blocks.title: Inserting 65 into the running tree
blocks.prompt: Insert the key 65 into the BST above, showing each comparison, and state where the new node lands and what the height becomes.

steps.text: Insertion always creates a leaf, so the algorithm walks down as if searching for 65 and attaches the node where the search falls off the tree. Start at the root.
At 50: $65 > 50$, so 65 must belong in the right subtree. Move to 70.
At 70: $65 < 70$, so 65 belongs in 70's left subtree. Move to 60.
At 60: $65 > 60$, so 65 belongs in 60's right subtree. But 60's right child is null — the search has fallen off the tree.
Attach 65 as the right child of 60. Three comparisons were made, one per node on the path.

Verify the invariant along the whole path, which is the only place it could break. 65 is in 50's right subtree and $65 > 50$; it is in 70's left subtree and $65 < 70$; it is in 60's right subtree and $65 > 60$. All three hold, so the tree is still a BST.

The resulting shape has 60 with a right child 65, so the path 50 → 70 → 60 → 65 has three edges and the height rises from 2 to 3. The in-order traversal is now 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 65, 70, 80 — still sorted, as it must be.

blocks.answer: 65 becomes the right child of 60, after three comparisons; the height increases from 2 to 3.

blocks.markdown:
## Traversals

The three depth-first traversals differ only in *when* the node itself is emitted relative to its subtrees. Each visits every node once, so each is $\Theta(n)$ time and $O(h)$ auxiliary space for the recursion stack.

```
inorder(v):   if v != null: inorder(v.left);  emit(v); inorder(v.right)
preorder(v):  if v != null: emit(v); preorder(v.left);  preorder(v.right)
postorder(v): if v != null: postorder(v.left); postorder(v.right); emit(v)
```

For the running tree:

| Traversal | Order | Output | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|
| In-order | left, node, right | 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80 | Reading keys in sorted order; validating the BST invariant |
| Pre-order | node, left, right | 50, 30, 20, 40, 70, 60, 80 | Serialising the tree; re-inserting in this order rebuilds the identical shape |
| Post-order | left, right, node | 20, 40, 30, 60, 80, 70, 50 | Freeing the tree; evaluating an expression tree bottom-up |
| Level-order | by increasing depth | 50, 30, 70, 20, 40, 60, 80 | Breadth-first printing; uses a queue, not recursion |

That in-order traversal yields sorted output is not a coincidence but a restatement of the invariant, and it gives an $O(n)$ correctness check: a binary tree is a BST if and only if its in-order output is strictly increasing.

### Deletion: three cases

Deletion is the only non-obvious operation, because removing an internal node leaves a hole that must be filled without breaking the ordering.

1. **Leaf.** Detach it. Nothing else changes.
2. **One child.** Splice the child into the removed node's position. The child's subtree already sits entirely on the correct side of every ancestor, so the invariant survives.
3. **Two children.** Neither child can simply be promoted. Instead copy the **in-order successor** — the minimum key of the right subtree, found by going right once then left as far as possible — into the node, then delete that successor from the right subtree. The successor has no left child by construction, so the recursive deletion is case 1 or case 2 and cannot recurse further.

The successor is the correct choice because it is the smallest key greater than the deleted one: every key remaining in the left subtree is still smaller, and every key remaining in the right subtree is still larger. The mirror-image choice, the in-order **predecessor** (maximum of the left subtree), is equally valid; alternating between the two is a cheap way to reduce the height skew that repeated deletions otherwise induce.

blocks.caption: Why the BST survives despite the hash table's faster lookup: only the ordered structures answer successor and range queries efficiently.

blocks.title: Sorted input is the worst case
blocks.text: Insert 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 in ascending order and every key becomes the right child of its predecessor. The result is a chain of height $n - 1$ on which every operation is $\Theta(n)$ — a linked list carrying a wasted null pointer per node. Since real data arrives sorted disturbingly often, an unbalanced BST is not a safe production structure.

blocks.markdown:
### Restoring the logarithmic guarantee

**Self-balancing** trees perform $O(1)$ local restructurings, called *rotations*, after each update to keep the height in $O(\log n)$:

- **AVL trees** require the two subtree heights of every node to differ by at most 1. The tightest balance, so the fastest lookups, at the cost of more rotations on update.
- **Red-black trees** enforce a colouring discipline that bounds the height by $2\log_2(n+1)$. Looser balance, fewer rotations — which is why they back most standard-library ordered maps.
- **B-trees** raise the branching factor to hundreds so that the height is 3 or 4 even for millions of keys, minimising disk or page reads. This is the structure behind essentially every relational database index.

A rotation changes the shape while preserving the in-order sequence exactly — which is the reason it cannot break the BST invariant.

points: Depth counts edges from the root down; height counts edges from a node to its deepest leaf, so a leaf has height 0.
A binary tree of height $h$ holds between $h+1$ and $2^{h+1}-1$ nodes, so $n$ nodes require height at least $\lceil \log_2(n+1) \rceil - 1$.
The BST invariant constrains entire subtrees, not just immediate children — the local-only version permits trees in which search fails.
Search and insertion walk one root-to-leaf path, so both cost $O(h)$; insertion always creates a leaf.
In-order traversal yields sorted output, pre-order serialises the shape, and post-order processes children before parents.
Deleting a node with two children copies in its in-order successor, the minimum of the right subtree, then deletes that successor.
Sorted insertion degenerates a BST into a chain of height $n-1$; AVL, red-black and B-trees use rotations to keep the height logarithmic.
